chapter.title: When it goes wrong: loops, made-up facts, and wrong turns

cards.body: Your intern has worked all morning and hands you a report. You cannot see what is in their head, but you can read the notes they kept: what they tried, what came back, what they did next. Interns go wrong in 3 ways. They repeat the same dead-end call 20 times. They write down a number nobody gave them. Or they do a beautiful job on the wrong task. Every agent failure you will meet is one of these 3.

cards.title: The 3 failure types
cards.body:
An agent log is the written record of the loop from chapter 2. Each line shows what the model decided (the think step), what tool ran (the act step), and what came back (the check step). Reading a log is how you find out where things went wrong, because the agent itself will often tell you it succeeded.

Failure 1 is the loop. The agent tries a step, it fails or returns nothing useful, and the agent tries the exact same step again. And again. It never changes its approach because each turn it only sees that the task is not done yet. You spot it when 2 or more lines are identical, or nearly identical.

Failure 2 is the made-up fact. The model requests a tool, the tool returns an error or an empty result, and the model carries on as if it got a real answer. It writes a price, a date, or a file name that never appeared in any tool result. You spot it by checking: does every fact in the final answer trace back to a line where a tool actually returned it?

Failure 3 is the wrong turn. Every step runs cleanly and every fact is real, but the agent misread the goal. Asked to find cheap flights to Lisbon, it researches Lisbon hotels. You spot it only by comparing the first line (the goal) with the last line (the result), because the middle will look fine.

The quickest diagnosis: a repeating log is a loop, a fact with no source line is made-up, a clean log answering a different question is a wrong turn.

cards.prompt: An agent's log shows the same line 6 times: 'Searching web for: company phone number'. No results came back each time. Which failure type is this?

options.text: The loop. It keeps repeating a step that does not work.
The made-up fact. It is inventing a phone number.
The wrong turn. It should not be searching at all.

whyNot.b: That's the made-up fact, not the loop: a made-up fact means a result appears that no tool gave. Here, nothing has been invented yet. It is just stuck.
whyNot.c: That's the wrong turn, not the loop: a wrong turn means the agent solved a different problem. Searching for a phone number matches the task fine. The problem is the repeating.

cards.reteach: A loop is when the agent does the same step over and over and never changes its plan. The giveaway is repetition in the log: identical or near-identical lines. The content of the step can be perfectly sensible. It is the repeating that is the failure.

cards.title: A 10-line log, read slowly
cards.body:
Goal: 'Find the opening hours of the Oak Street library and add them to my notes file.' Line 2: the model asks the web search tool for 'Oak Street library hours'. Line 3: the tool returns an error, 'connection timed out'. Line 4: the model writes: 'The library is open 9am to 6pm, Monday to Saturday.' Line 5: it asks the file tool to append that text to notes.txt. Line 6: the file tool says 'done'. Line 7: the model reports 'Task complete.'

The log looks tidy and it finished in 7 steps. But line 3 gave an error and line 4 states hours that no tool ever returned. That is a made-up fact, and it is now sitting in a real file.

cards.title: Why the tidy ones are the dangerous ones
cards.body:
Loops are the easiest failure to catch. They burn time and money, but they rarely do damage, because nothing new gets done. Many agents have a step cap for exactly this reason, which chapter 6 covers.

Made-up facts and wrong turns are worse because the log ends with 'Task complete'. The intern is confident. The only defence is the habit of tracing: pick each fact in the final answer and find the exact log line where a tool handed it over. If you cannot find that line, the fact was invented.

For a wrong turn, you trace differently. You reread the goal in line 1, then read the final result, and ask whether a stranger would say they match. Skip the middle at first. The middle is where the agent looks competent, which is exactly what fools you.

cards.prompt: Goal: 'Email the 3 newest invoices to the accountant.' The log shows the agent searched the inbox, found 3 invoices from last year, attached them, and sent the email. Every tool call succeeded. Which failure is this?

options.text: The loop. It did 3 of the same thing.
The wrong turn. The invoices were real but they were not the newest.
The made-up fact. The invoices did not exist.

whyNot.a: That's the loop, not the wrong turn: a loop repeats a step without progress. Attaching 3 different files is progress, not repetition.
whyNot.c: That's the made-up fact, not the wrong turn: made-up means a tool never returned it. The inbox tool really did return those invoices. They were just the wrong ones.

cards.reteach: A wrong turn is a clean run at the wrong target. Every tool call succeeds and every fact is real, but the result does not match the goal. You catch it by holding the first line and the last line side by side, not by checking the steps in between.

cards.body: The common mistake is trusting the last line. 'Task complete' is the model's opinion, not a tool's report, and the model writes it after made-up facts and wrong turns too. Spot the habit in yourself: if you only read the final message and not the tool results above it, you are grading the intern on their own self-review.

cards.prompt: Which check catches a made-up fact in an agent log?

options.text: Look for the same step repeated several times.
Compare the goal in line 1 with the final result.
Find the tool result line that gave each fact in the answer.

whyNot.a: That's the check for a loop, not a made-up fact: repetition shows the agent is stuck, not that it invented something.
whyNot.b: That's the check for a wrong turn, not a made-up fact: matching goal to result catches a misread task, but a made-up fact can appear in an answer that matches the goal perfectly.

cards.reteach: A made-up fact is a claim with no source. The model wrote it, but no tool returned it. So the test is to take each fact in the final answer and look upward in the log for the tool line that produced it. No line, no source, made up.

cards.body: Ask any chatbot you use for a fact it cannot know, like today's weather in a small town. Notice whether it says 'I cannot check' or confidently invents one. That is the made-up fact habit in miniature.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now read a short agent log, point to the line where it went wrong, and name it as a loop, a made-up fact, or a wrong turn.
